newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: CHH sees better outlook for pulp prices.
newsitem.headline: CHH sees better outlook for pulp prices.

text.p: Carter Holt Harvey Ltd chief executive John Faraci said on Tuesday the fundamentals for pulp prices were now better than in the third quarter of the last financial year.
"I believe the fundamentals now are better for a pulp price increase that will stick, relative to fundamentals in the third quarter of last year when prices didn't stick," he told a news conference.
Faraci said inventory levels had eased lower, but were still somewhat high.

He said Australia remained the company's focus for future growth, and the recent acquisition of Sydney-based Australian Plastics Industries gave CHH's plastics packaging business a platform for further grow and better service its trans-Tasman markets.

Earnings before interest and tax fell to NZ$350 million against $545 million, reflecting difficult trading conditions in all major markets and ongoing price pressure across all products. Pretax profit fell to $246 million from $442.
"In spite of this, the company was able to achieve solid progress on controllable factors such as sales volumes and costs," Faraci said.

In its statement the company said it had lost about $246 million through the impact of pricing effects while on the otherhand the combination of sales volume and cost controls had offset $70 million of this effect.
He said the results represented cyclical lows in its major markets.
"However, the fundamentals for the medium term remain sound."
Faraci said he expected improvements in pulp and paper prices to flow through this June, July and August.
Harvest volumes were 4.9 million tonnes, up six percent on the previous year. Sales of saw logs to domestic customers increased by eight percent.
Prices in export markets were weak.
Both the Korean and Japanese economies were soft, with additional pressure from the weakening of those currencies against the U.S. dollar, the company added.

Faraci told the news conference that he was neither optimistic nor pessimistic about log markets in Asia, although he said there were concerns about the Korean economy as that country went through a restructuring.
He said the wood products markets in Australia should improve.
"Lower building activity in Australia continued to impact on profitability, but some improvement has been seen in the March 1997 quarter and recent price increases have been held," Faraci said.
Earnings from associated companies in the year to March fell to NZ$75 million from $126 million, mostly due to reduced earnings from COPEC.
